questions.prompt: Which statement most accurately reflects this course's position on quantum machine learning's current practical status?
options: QML is an active, legitimate research area with real theoretical results but no peer-reviewed, independently reproduced demonstration of practical advantage over classical ML on real-world tasks
QML has already been proven to outperform classical ML on most real-world business problems
QML is purely theoretical and no QML circuit can be run on any hardware or simulator today
QML has been mathematically proven to never provide any benefit over classical ML under any circumstances
questions.explain: The course's precise, repeatedly-stated position is that QML has genuine theoretical interest and runnable circuits, but no fair, reproduced, practically-relevant demonstration of advantage exists today -- neither hype nor dismissal is accurate.
questions.distractorExplain: Options B and D both overclaim in opposite directions -- B claims a proven advantage that doesn't exist, D claims an impossibility that has never been proven either. Option C is also false since every lab in this course runs real, simulatable circuits.

questions.prompt: Select every pattern this course's Lesson 4 identifies as a common way QML papers or marketing overclaim results.
options: Comparing against a weak or outdated classical baseline instead of a strong, tuned one
Citing a theoretical fault-tolerant speedup as though it applies directly to current NISQ hardware
Ignoring the classical cost of simulating a small quantum circuit when claiming an advantage
Using a classical baseline tuned with comparable hyperparameter search effort to the quantum model
Showing an 'advantage' only at a toy dataset size that happens to flatter the quantum method
questions.explain: Weak baselines, misapplied fault-tolerant speedup claims, ignored simulation costs, and cherry-picked dataset sizes are all explicitly named overclaiming patterns. A comparably-tuned classical baseline is the opposite -- it's exactly what a FAIR comparison requires.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the process of finding a classical algorithm that matches a claimed quantum speedup, removing the advantage, is called ________.
questions.explain: Dequantization describes exactly this pattern -- several mid-2010s exponential QML speedup claims were later matched by classical algorithms, removing the claimed advantage.

questions.prompt: What did Google's 2019 Sycamore 'quantum supremacy' experiment actually demonstrate?
options: A quantum processor sampling faster from a specific, contrived random circuit's output distribution than a classical supercomputer could simulate -- a deliberately non-practical task
A quantum computer outperforming a classical model on a real-world machine learning benchmark
The first fully fault-tolerant, error-corrected quantum computation at useful scale
A quantum kernel method beating a tuned classical SVM on image classification
questions.explain: The Sycamore experiment used a contrived random-circuit sampling task chosen specifically to demonstrate a measurable quantum-vs-classical computational gap -- it has no practical application and is not an ML result of any kind.

questions.prompt: Select every component that is part of the standard variational quantum circuit anatomy covered in Lesson 5.
options: State preparation / encoding of classical data
A parameterized ansatz with trainable gate angles
Measurement producing an expectation value or sampled outcome
A classical feedback loop that updates parameters based on the loss
A built-in classical neural network layer fused inside the quantum circuit itself
questions.explain: The four-part anatomy is encode, parameterize (ansatz), measure, and classically feed back/update. There is no such thing as a classical neural network layer 'fused inside' the quantum circuit -- classical and quantum computation remain separate, connected only through measurement outcomes and parameter updates.

questions.prompt: For the single-qubit circuit RY(theta)|0>, measuring the Pauli-Z observable gives <Z>(theta) = cos(theta) exactly. Using the parameter-shift rule [f(theta+pi/2) - f(theta-pi/2)]/2 at theta = pi/3, what is the computed gradient, to 3 decimal places?
questions.explain: f(pi/3+pi/2)=cos(5pi/6)=-0.866 and f(pi/3-pi/2)=cos(-pi/6)=0.866, giving (-0.866-0.866)/2=-0.866, which exactly matches the analytic derivative -sin(pi/3)=-0.866.

questions.prompt: Why is the parameter-shift rule's shift of exactly pi/2 fundamentally different from a classical finite-difference step size epsilon?
options: Pi/2 gives an EXACT gradient for Pauli-generated rotation gates, not an approximation that only improves as epsilon shrinks toward zero like classical finite differences
Pi/2 is simply the smallest step size that happens to fit on NISQ hardware today
There is no real difference; pi/2 is just a conventional default choice for epsilon
Classical finite-difference methods also always use exactly pi/2 as their step size
questions.explain: Parameter-shift is exact at pi/2 for gates generated by an operator with eigenvalues +-1/2, unlike classical finite differences which only approximate the derivative and get noisier as epsilon shrinks on real hardware.

questions.prompt: Select every factor this course's Lesson 8 identifies as worsening the barren plateau effect.
options: More qubits (the exponential gradient-variance shrinkage is specifically in qubit count)
Deeper, more expressive ansatze that approach the full Haar-random state space
Random parameter initialization, the regime McClean et al.'s original proof covers
Global cost functions / observables measured across all qubits
Using fewer trainable parameters than the number of qubits in the circuit
questions.explain: More qubits, deeper/more expressive ansatze, random initialization, and global cost functions are all documented contributing factors. Parameter-to-qubit count ratio alone is not one of the factors the lesson identifies.

questions.prompt: A barren plateau and the classical 'vanishing gradient' problem in deep neural networks are both 'gradient disappears as scale increases' problems. According to Lesson 8, how do they differ?
options: They arise from different mathematical mechanisms -- barren plateaus from the expressibility of the reachable quantum state space, classical vanishing gradients from repeated multiplication of small derivatives through many layers
They are mathematically identical phenomena with no meaningful difference
Barren plateaus only occur in classical neural networks, never in quantum circuits
Vanishing gradients only occur in quantum circuits, never in classical neural networks
questions.explain: Both are conceptually similar failure modes (gradients vanish as scale grows) but are mathematically distinct: barren plateaus come from how much of the Haar-random state space an expressive circuit can reach, while classical vanishing gradients come from repeatedly multiplying small derivatives through depth.

questions.prompt: Amplitude-encoding the classical vector (3, 4) into a single qubit gives which normalized quantum state?
options: 3|0> + 4|1>, left unnormalized
questions.explain: The vector (3,4) has norm sqrt(9+16)=5, so normalizing gives (3/5, 4/5) = (0.6, 0.8), and 0.6^2+0.8^2=1.0 confirms this is a valid quantum state.
questions.distractorExplain: Option D swaps the amplitudes' order (0.8 then 0.6), which would instead correspond to amplitude-encoding the vector (4,3), not (3,4) -- order matters since amplitude encoding preserves each original value's position.

questions.prompt: Using single-qubit angle encoding, the quantum kernel simplifies to k(x,x') = cos^2((x-x')/2). What is k(0.4, 1.2), to 4 decimal places?
questions.explain: cos((0.4-1.2)/2) = cos(-0.4) is approximately 0.9211, and squaring gives approximately 0.8484 -- confirmed by both the closed-form formula and the long-hand inner product calculation.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about angle encoding versus amplitude encoding, per Lessons 10-11.
options: Angle encoding needs one qubit per feature; amplitude encoding needs only log2(N) qubits for N classical values
Amplitude encoding's qubit savings can be partly or fully offset by a higher gate count needed to prepare an arbitrary state
Angle encoding's circuit depth for state preparation is effectively constant regardless of feature count
Amplitude encoding always requires fewer total gates than angle encoding, with no exceptions
Basis encoding needs exactly one qubit per classical bit
questions.explain: Angle encoding is one-qubit-per-feature with constant depth; amplitude encoding is exponentially qubit-efficient but can require a gate count that grows with the number of amplitudes, which can offset or exceed angle encoding's gate cost -- so amplitude encoding does NOT always need fewer total gates.

questions.prompt: An SVM never needs the explicit feature vectors used by a quantum kernel method. What does it actually need, and why does this make a quantum kernel a drop-in replacement?
options: It only needs the kernel matrix K[i][j] = k(xi, xj) for every pair of training points -- computing that matrix via a quantum circuit changes nothing about how the SVM's margin-maximization, support vectors, or regularization work
It needs the raw classical feature vectors directly, which a quantum kernel cannot provide
It needs a fully trained neural network to generate the kernel matrix
Quantum kernels cannot be used with SVMs under any circumstances
questions.explain: SVM theory operates entirely on the kernel matrix, never on explicit feature vectors, which is exactly why swapping in a quantum-computed kernel matrix requires zero changes to the SVM itself -- the only quantum part is computing K.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a failure mode where quantum kernel values cluster near a constant as qubit count grows, losing the ability to discriminate between data points, is called kernel ________.
questions.explain: Kernel concentration is a documented cousin of the barren plateau problem -- as qubits scale up, some natural quantum kernel constructions lose discriminative power because values cluster near a constant.

questions.prompt: What is the real structural distinction this course draws between the terms 'QNN' and 'VQC'?
options: A difference of architectural emphasis and naming convention -- QNN usually implies a deeper stack of layers by analogy to classical network depth, not a structurally different training algorithm
QNNs use an entirely different training algorithm with no parameter-shift gradients involved at all
VQCs can only be used for regression tasks; QNNs can only be used for classification
QNN refers exclusively to real quantum hardware implementations, never to simulations
questions.explain: Both terms use the identical encode-ansatz-measure-loss-gradient-update loop; QNN is typically reserved for deeper layer stacks motivated by analogy to classical deep learning, not a different underlying algorithm.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about why quantum circuits lack a clean analogue of a classical nonlinear activation function.
options: Quantum states evolve linearly (unitarily) between measurements, with no natural gate behaving like a classical nonlinear activation
Classical deep networks collapse into a single linear transformation without nonlinear activations between layers, regardless of depth
Entangling gates introduce complexity in the correlations a circuit can represent, even though the underlying operators remain linear
This is purely a software limitation of PennyLane and Qiskit that will be patched in a future library update
Mid-circuit measurement and post-processing is one proposed workaround, at the cost of extra circuit complexity
questions.explain: The lack of a quantum nonlinear activation analogue is a genuine physical/mathematical property of unitary evolution, not a software gap -- entangling gates and mid-circuit measurement are real, documented partial workarounds, each with real costs.

questions.prompt: In a 2-qubit circuit with a CNOT gate (control=qubit 1, target=qubit 2), a fact proven in Lesson 18's lab is that the CNOT never changes which qubit's own marginal measurement probabilities? Answer with just the word 'control' or 'target'.
questions.explain: A CNOT only permutes amplitudes within the block where the control is |1>, which can never move probability between the control being |0> and |1> -- so the control qubit's own marginal is always unchanged by that CNOT, while the target qubit's marginal does change.

questions.prompt: What specific, legitimate result did Cong, Choi, and Lukin (2019) actually demonstrate for Quantum Convolutional Neural Networks (QCNNs)?
options: QCNNs can efficiently recognize certain quantum error-correcting code phases and quantum many-body phases of matter -- a task classifying quantum data, not classical images
QCNNs outperform classical CNNs on standard classical image classification benchmarks
QCNNs eliminate the need for any classical optimizer during training
QCNNs require zero qubits, running the entire computation classically
questions.explain: The original QCNN result is specifically about classifying quantum-native data (phases of matter), a real and useful but narrow result -- it is not evidence of any advantage on classical image classification tasks.

questions.prompt: Why can't the entire QML training loop, including the optimizer, run on quantum hardware with zero classical computation?
options: There is no known way to run gradient aggregation and optimizer state updates (e.g., Adam's running averages) as a quantum circuit -- that arithmetic is classical because only classical hardware currently does it efficiently
Quantum hardware is physically incapable of storing any numeric values whatsoever
Classical and quantum computers are not permitted to communicate under any current protocol
The parameter-shift rule can only be computed by a classical computer, never on real quantum hardware
questions.explain: Optimizer logic has no known quantum-circuit implementation, which is exactly why every practical QML training approach today is hybrid -- the circuit runs on quantum hardware/simulator, but the optimizer update is always classical.

questions.prompt: For a circuit with k trainable parameters trained via the parameter-shift rule, how many total quantum-side circuit evaluations does ONE full gradient step require? Answer in terms of k (e.g., 'k' or '2k').
questions.explain: Each parameter needs its own plus-shift and minus-shift evaluation, giving 2k total circuit evaluations for one full gradient -- a real practical bottleneck compared to classical backprop's roughly single-extra-pass cost.

questions.prompt: Select every item on this course's 'should we build a hybrid model' decision checklist from Lesson 21.
options: Is there a credible, specific reason to expect this quantum component to help, beyond general curiosity?
What is the realistic qubit/parameter budget, and does it fit comfortably without hitting barren plateaus?
What is the added latency and cost, including classical simulation cost for larger circuits?
Is there a strong classical baseline already in hand, tuned with comparable effort?
Has the marketing team approved using the word 'quantum' in promotional materials?
questions.explain: The checklist covers specific expected mechanism, qubit/parameter budget versus barren-plateau risk, latency/cost, and classical baseline strength -- marketing approval is not a technical engineering consideration the lesson includes.

questions.prompt: In PennyLane's TorchLayer, how does the quantum layer's gradient become available to PyTorch's autograd system during the backward pass?
options: TorchLayer internally runs the parameter-shift gradient computation and returns the result to autograd as if it came from ordinary backpropagation -- autograd doesn't need to know the underlying method differed
It requires the user to manually compute and inject the gradient at every single training step
It disables autograd entirely for any model containing a quantum layer
It converts the quantum circuit into a static lookup table computed once before training begins
questions.explain: TorchLayer handles the parameter-shift computation internally and hands the result back to autograd in the expected format, which is what makes dropping a QNode into a PyTorch model work without hand-written hybrid-loop code.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: data not used during training, used afterward to check whether a model actually generalizes, is called the ________ set.
questions.explain: A held-out (test) set is data never used during training, specifically kept aside to measure whether a trained model generalizes rather than just memorizing training examples.

questions.prompt: Why does the course's Chapter 6 project choose the real Iris dataset (reduced to 2 features, 2 classes) rather than a brand-new, never-before-studied dataset?
options: A well-characterized, publicly documented dataset lets the classical baseline comparison be fairly and meaningfully evaluated against results the field already understands, satisfying Lesson 4's fair-comparison standard
Iris is the only dataset that can be angle-encoded with any number of qubits
Brand-new datasets are mathematically impossible to load into PennyLane or Qiskit Machine Learning
Iris was specifically designed and collected for quantum computing research
questions.explain: Using a well-documented, widely-used benchmark means results are comparable to existing published and tutorial work -- a novel dataset would have no established classical track record to sanity-check the comparison against.

questions.prompt: In the Chapter 6 project's benchmark (Lesson 25), the classical threshold-rule baseline achieved what accuracy on the 6-sample held-out set? Answer as a percentage (e.g., '50%').
questions.explain: The simple petal-length threshold rule correctly classified all 6 held-out samples (3 Setosa, 3 Versicolor), for 100% accuracy -- a genuinely strong, if trivial, classical baseline for this near-linearly-separable task.

questions.prompt: Select every accurate explanation for why the Chapter 6 project's quantum classifier predicted class 0 for every held-out sample, including all three Versicolor samples.
options: The single gradient-descent step in Lesson 24 was computed using only the Setosa sample, so training only ever pushed parameters toward correctly classifying Setosa
The model never received any training signal that would help it separate Versicolor from Setosa, since Versicolor's loss and gradient were never computed during the one training step taken
This reflects a fundamental, unfixable limitation of all quantum circuits, proven mathematically in Chapter 2
A real multi-sample, multi-iteration training run updating both theta1 and theta2 together would very plausibly close most of this gap on this near-linearly-separable task
questions.explain: The failure is specifically traceable to undertraining (one sample, one step, one parameter) -- not a fundamental, unfixable quantum limitation. A genuine multi-sample training run would very plausibly fix most of the issue, since Setosa/Versicolor is an easy classification task for almost any reasonable classifier.

questions.prompt: What does the Chapter 6 project's final benchmark result (classical 100% vs. quantum 50%) honestly license concluding, per Lesson 26?
options: That a quantum classifier trained on one sample for one step underperforms a trivial classical rule on this specific task -- not that QML underperforms classical ML in general or that a properly-trained version would necessarily fail too
That quantum machine learning has now been conclusively proven inferior to classical machine learning for all tasks
That the classical threshold rule is mathematically guaranteed to work on every possible dataset
That barren plateaus caused this specific result
questions.explain: The lesson is explicit that this narrow, specific, honestly-scoped finding does not generalize to a verdict on QML broadly -- and barren plateaus specifically require many more qubits than this 2-qubit toy circuit has, so that's not the explanation for this particular result either.

questions.prompt: Select every item this course's toolchain lesson (Lesson 3) correctly attributes to PennyLane versus Qiskit Machine Learning.
options: PennyLane's QNode treats a quantum circuit as a differentiable function bound to a device
Qiskit ML's VQC bundles a feature map, ansatz, and optimizer behind a scikit-learn-style .fit()/.predict() interface
PennyLane plugs directly into PyTorch, TensorFlow, and JAX for hybrid model integration
Qiskit Machine Learning cannot be used with any classical simulator, only real IBM hardware
Both libraries ultimately rely on the same underlying math: state preparation, ansatz, measurement, and parameter-shift gradients
questions.explain: QNode, VQC's packaged interface, and PennyLane's ML-framework interoperability are all accurately described; Qiskit ML works extensively with the AerSimulator and other classical simulators, so claiming it only works on real hardware is false.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: on real or shot-based-simulated hardware, an expectation value is a statistical estimate from a finite number of circuit repetitions rather than an exact number -- this added noise source is called ________ noise.
questions.explain: Shot noise is the statistical noise arising from using a finite number of circuit repetitions ('shots') to estimate an expectation value -- an additional noise source that classical ML training doesn't have, and which can compound with barren-plateau effects.

questions.prompt: Why does this course treat data encoding (basis, angle, or amplitude) as part of the QML model itself, rather than a neutral preprocessing step like classical feature scaling?
options: The encoding choice determines the actual geometry of the quantum states the circuit can access, directly constraining what patterns the ansatz or a quantum kernel can later detect
Encoding has no real effect on anything downstream and is purely a cosmetic labeling choice
Classical feature scaling and quantum encoding are mathematically identical operations
Encoding only matters for basis encoding; angle and amplitude encoding have no effect on model behavior
questions.explain: Unlike classical feature scaling, the encoding choice changes the fundamental geometry of accessible quantum states -- two circuits with identical ansatze but different encodings are meaningfully different models, which is why Lesson 11 dedicates a full comparison to this choice.
